title: Let the Computer Roll the Dice
objective: After this level you can explain how running thousands of pretend trials on a computer estimates a chance too hard to calculate.
summary: A Monte Carlo simulation estimates a chance by running many random pretend trials and counting the successes. Stanislaw Ulam had the idea over solitaire in 1946; it first ran on ENIAC in 1948.

cards.headline: In 1946, a mathematician recovering from illness got stuck on solitaire.
cards.body: Stanislaw Ulam wanted the chance that a hand of 52 cards would come out. Working it out exactly was monstrously hard. His way around the math now runs on computers everywhere.

cards.headline: Don't calculate. Deal.
cards.body: Ulam's idea: instead of doing the math, lay the cards out a hundred times and count how many games come out. Successes divided by tries estimates the chance. Each game has to start from a fresh random shuffle, and the more tries you run, the closer the share tends to get to the true chance. That's a Monte Carlo simulation: lots of pretend trials, then count.

cards.headline: Named after a casino
cards.body: Ulam talked it over with John von Neumann, and they saw it could crack hard problems in their work at Los Alamos, like tracing the paths of neutrons. A colleague, Nick Metropolis, named it Monte Carlo, after the casino town Ulam's uncle kept borrowing money to visit. The first runs were on the ENIAC computer in 1948.

cards.fact: A simulation convinced Paul Erdős about Monty Hall.
cards.context: The great mathematician reportedly doubted Level 36's answer until computer simulations confirmed it. You could do the same: play 3,000 pretend games, always switching, and you'd expect to win about 2,000. Today the same trick measures risks in science, finance, transport, health and manufacturing.

cards.headline: Simulation: understood
learned: Too hard to calculate? Run pretend trials and count
Simulations settled Monty Hall for Erdős

questions.prompt: The idea behind the Monte Carlo method came to _____ while playing solitaire in 1946.

options.label: John von Neumann
options.rationale: He helped develop and program it after Ulam described it.

options.label: Nick Metropolis
options.rationale: He gave the method its name.

options.label: Paul Erdős
options.rationale: He was convinced about Monty Hall by simulations.

questions.explanation: Stanislaw Ulam wondered about a solitaire hand while recovering from illness in 1946.

questions.prompt: How does a Monte Carlo simulation estimate a chance?

options.label: It runs many random trials and counts the share that succeed
It looks up the answer in a table of known probabilities
options.rationale: It is used when no one can work the answer out.

options.label: It plays once and reports what happened
options.rationale: One trial tells you little; it runs many.

options.label: It averages the best and worst possible outcomes
options.rationale: It counts successes over many random trials.

questions.explanation: Successes divided by tries estimates the chance, and more tries tend to bring it closer.

questions.prompt: A computer plays 3,000 Monty Hall games, always switching. About how many should it win?

options.label: About 1,000
options.rationale: That's what always staying would win.

options.label: About 1,500
options.rationale: That assumes the last two doors are 50-50.

options.label: About 3,000
options.rationale: Switching loses whenever the first pick was the car.

questions.explanation: Switching wins 2 times in 3, and 2 in 3 of 3,000 is 2,000.
